paragraphs: He was truly distressed, more than he had been in a long time. He had rushed in like a fool, and meddled in what? A love affair. “But what do I know about it? What can I tell about such things?” he repeated to himself for the hundredth time, flushing crimson. “Oh, being ashamed would be nothing; shame is only the punishment I deserve. The trouble is that I’ve certainly caused more unhappiness.... And Father Zossima sent me to reconcile them and bring them together. Is this how to bring them together?” Then he suddenly remembered how he had tried to join their hands, and he felt terribly ashamed again. “I acted quite sincerely, but I must be more sensible in the future,” he concluded suddenly, and did not even smile at his conclusion.

Katerina Ivanovna’s errand took him to Lake Street, and his brother Dmitri lived close by, in a side street off Lake Street. Alyosha decided to go to him in any case before going to the captain, though he had a feeling that he wouldn’t find his brother. He suspected that Dmitri would keep out of his way on purpose now, but he had to find him anyhow. Time was passing: he had not stopped thinking of his dying elder for a single minute since he left the monastery.

One point in Katerina Ivanovna’s errand interested him particularly. When she mentioned the captain’s son, the little schoolboy who had run beside his father crying, the thought had struck Alyosha at once that this must be the schoolboy who had bitten his finger when he, Alyosha, asked him what he had done to hurt him. Now Alyosha felt almost certain of this, though he couldn’t have said why. Thinking about something else was a relief, and he resolved to stop thinking about the “mischief” he had done and not to torture himself with remorse, but to do what he had to do, come what may. That thought comforted him completely. As he turned into the street where Dmitri lodged, he felt hungry, so he took out of his pocket the roll he had brought from his father’s and ate it. It made him feel stronger.

Dmitri was not at home. The people of the house, an old cabinet-maker, his son and his old wife, looked at Alyosha with downright suspicion. “He hasn’t slept here for the last three nights. Maybe he’s gone away,” the old man said in answer to Alyosha’s persistent questions. Alyosha saw that he was answering on instructions. When he asked whether Dmitri might be at Grushenka’s, or in hiding at Foma’s (Alyosha spoke so freely on purpose), all three looked at him in alarm. “They’re fond of him, they’re doing their best for him,” thought Alyosha. “That’s good.”

At last he found the house in Lake Street. It was a decrepit little house, sunk on one side, with three windows looking onto the street, and a muddy yard with a single cow standing in the middle of it. He crossed the yard and found the door that opened into the passage. On the left of the passage lived the old woman of the house with her old daughter. Both seemed to be deaf. He asked again and again for the captain, until one of them finally understood that he was asking for their lodgers, and pointed to a door across the passage. The captain’s lodging turned out to be a plain cottage room. Alyosha had his hand on the iron latch to open the door when he was struck by the strange hush inside. Yet he knew from Katerina Ivanovna’s words that the man had a family. “Either they’re all asleep, or perhaps they’ve heard me coming and are waiting for me to open the door. I’d better knock first,” he thought, and knocked. An answer came, but not at once, after a pause of perhaps ten seconds.
“Who’s there?” someone shouted, in a loud and very angry voice.

Then Alyosha opened the door and stepped inside. He found himself in a regular peasant’s room. Though it was large, it was cluttered with household belongings of all sorts, and there were several people in it. On the left was a large Russian stove. From the stove to the window on the left a string ran across the room, with rags hanging on it. There was a bedstead against the wall on each side, right and left, covered with knitted quilts. On the one on the left was a pyramid of four print-covered pillows, each smaller than the one beneath. On the other there was only one very small pillow. The opposite corner was screened off by a curtain or a sheet hung on a string. Behind this curtain a bed made up on a bench could be seen, and a chair. The rough square table of plain wood had been moved to the middle window. The three windows, each made of four tiny, greenish, mildewed panes, let in little light and were shut tight, so the room was rather dim and stuffy. On the table was a frying pan with the remains of some fried eggs, a half-eaten piece of bread, and a small bottle with a few drops of vodka.

A woman of genteel appearance, in a cotton gown, was sitting on a chair by the bed on the left. Her face was thin and yellow, and her sunken cheeks showed at first glance that she was ill. But what struck Alyosha most was the look in the poor woman’s eyes—a look of surprised inquiry and yet of haughty pride. And while he was talking to her husband, her big brown eyes moved from one speaker to the other with the same haughty, questioning look. Beside her at the window stood a young girl, rather plain, with scanty reddish hair, poorly but very neatly dressed. She looked at Alyosha with disdain as he came in. Beside the other bed sat another female figure. She was a very sad sight, a young girl of about twenty, but hunchbacked and crippled, “with withered legs,” as Alyosha was told afterwards. Her crutches stood in the corner close by. The strikingly beautiful, gentle eyes of this poor girl looked at Alyosha with mild serenity. A man of forty-five was sitting at the table, finishing the fried eggs. He was thin, small and weakly built. He had reddish hair and a scanty light-colored beard, very much like a wisp of tow (this comparison and the phrase “a wisp of tow” flashed into Alyosha’s mind at once, for some reason; he remembered it afterwards). Obviously this was the gentleman who had shouted to him, as there was no other man in the room. But when Alyosha came in, he leapt up from the bench on which he was sitting and, hastily wiping his mouth with a ragged napkin, darted up to Alyosha.
“It’s a monk come to beg for the monastery. A nice place to come to!” the girl standing in the left corner said aloud. The man spun round to her at once and answered in an excited, breaking voice:
“No, Varvara, you’re wrong. Allow me to ask,” he turned to Alyosha again, “what has brought you to—our retreat?”

Alyosha looked at him attentively. It was the first time he had seen him. There was something angular, flustered and irritable about him. Though he had obviously just been drinking, he was not drunk. There was extraordinary impudence in his expression, and yet, strange to say, there was fear in it too. He looked like a man who had long been kept in subjection and had put up with it, and who had now suddenly turned and was trying to assert himself. Or, better still, like a man who badly wants to hit you but is terribly afraid you will hit him. In his words and in the tone of his shrill voice there was a sort of crazy humor, at times spiteful and at times cringing, and constantly shifting from one tone to another. He had asked the question about “our retreat” quivering all over, rolling his eyes, and skipping up so close to Alyosha that he instinctively drew back a step. He was dressed in a very shabby dark cotton coat, patched and spotted. He wore checked trousers of an extremely light color, long out of fashion, and of very thin material. They were so crumpled and so short that he looked as though he had grown out of them like a boy.
“I am Alexey Karamazov,” Alyosha began in reply.
“I understand that perfectly, sir,” the gentleman snapped out at once, to assure him that he already knew who he was. “I am Captain Snegiryov, sir, but I still want to know exactly what has led you—”
“Oh, I’ve come for nothing special. I wanted to have a word with you—if you’ll allow me.”

“In that case, here is a chair, sir; kindly be seated. That’s what they used to say in the old comedies, ‘kindly be seated,’” and with a quick movement he seized an empty chair (a rough wooden chair, not upholstered) and set it for him almost in the middle of the room. Then, taking another chair like it for himself, he sat down facing Alyosha, so close that their knees almost touched.

“Nikolay Ilyitch Snegiryov, sir, formerly a captain in the Russian infantry, put to shame for his vices, but still a captain. Though I might not be one now, judging by the way I talk. For the last half of my life I’ve learned to say ‘sir.’ It’s a word you use when you’ve come down in the world.”
“That’s very true,” smiled Alyosha. “But does it come out without your meaning it, or do you say it on purpose?”
